claims.text: The starting material is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 prepared by powder consolidation.
The intervention is addition of 0.5 wt% Y2O3 nanoparticles.
The Y2O3 nanoparticles are to be introduced by mechanical alloying before sintering.
The proposed processing route will produce a uniform Y2O3 dispersion at grain boundaries and within grains.
Dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles will act as sinks for radiation-induced point defects.
Dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles will act as sinks for radiation-induced dislocation loops.
Absorption of irradiation defects by Y2O3 will mitigate the solute supersaturation that drives radiation-induced precipitation.
At approximately 8 dpa and 500°C, Y2O3 addition will reduce radiation-induced precipitation by more than 50% relative to the unmodified alloy.
At approximately 8 dpa and 500°C, the modified alloy will maintain or slightly reduce the negligible irradiation hardening of the unmodified alloy.
The unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy exhibits measurable radiation-induced precipitation at approximately 8 dpa and 500°C.
The unmodified alloy exhibits minimal irradiation hardening at approximately 8 dpa and 500°C.
Oxide-dispersion-strengthened processing routes will improve the alloy's bulk fabricability and processing scalability.
Approximately 1800°C is a suitable sintering temperature for the proposed modified and unmodified specimens.
An irradiation temperature around 500°C is relevant to fusion service.
The predicted benefit is conditional on maintaining a uniform nanoparticle dispersion without agglomeration.
Oxide dispersions are known to mitigate irradiation-defect accumulation in similar alloy systems.
